sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
On October 31, 2002 an earthquake having a Mw 5.8 occurs in the Molise region. The day after, a further earthquake with Mw 5.7 happens 8 kilometers to the west of the first one. The two seismic events are similar, in terms of hypocentral depths, focal mechanisms, source kinematics, and their slip patterns are almost contiguous.
The Italian seismicity is often characterized by multishock sequences, with at least two main earthquakes of similar magnitude, and very similar properties, such as observed for e.g. the Irpinia 1980 earthquakes, Friuli 1976 earthquakes, and Potenza 1990 events.
The two earthquake hypocenters are located at mid-crustal depths (ca. 16-20 km), and their mechanisms are almost pure strike-slip (Pondrelli et al., 2004). The analysis of the aftershock activity shows that the causative faults are the E-W striking ones. Aftershocks well define two sub-vertical, dextral strike-slip fault segments, in agreement with the mainshock fault plane solutions (Chiarabba et al., 2005). A large number of aftershocks focal mechanisms show a sub-horizontal NW and NE-trending P and T axes, respectively (Chiarabba et al., 2005).
Both earthquakes exhibit a clear updip rupture propagation, and a strong directivity effect, which amplified the radiation in the direction of the rupture propagation (Vallee and Di Luccio, 2005).
The 2002 seismic events were mostly unexpected by seismologists and geologists. In fact, the seismic sequence highlights the existence of active faulting in an area where neither historical/instrumental events have been previuosly recorded or seismogenic faults identified. The 2002 sequence area is located about 50 km east of the extensional Apenninic belt, and about 50 km west of the dextral strike-slip Mattinata Fault, an important crustal structure with a long tectonic history.
On-strike and eastward, an E-W trending fault system has also been observed offshore (e.g. Ridente et al., 2008).
The 2002 earthquakes may help to explain several large yet poorly understood historical earthquakes located between the crest of the Apennines and the Adriatic coastline (Valensise et al., 2004; Fracassi and Valensise, 2007). Striking similarities exist with the 1990 Potenza sequence (Mw 5.7), which ruptured at 15-25 km depth on E-W trending right-lateral strike slip faults, about 130 km south-east of the 2002 sequence.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) What is the average return period of this Source?
2) Is the E-W fault system containing the 2002 Molise earthquakes and the Mattinata Fault entirely seismogenic?
3) Does this E-W fault system rupture only in repeated events with M around 5.7, or can it rupture also in larger events?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Di Bucci and Mazzoli (2003)
They suggest that the Molise sequence is related to foreland deformation affecting the Adriatic lithosphere. Such deformation is characterised by active NW-SE compression, resulting in the reactivation of pre-existing east-west oriented structures as dextral strike-slip faults.
Valensise et al. (2004)
They show that the 2002 Molise earthquakes were caused by pure right-lateral slip between 10 and 24 km depth over a nearly vertical, previously undetected east-west fault. This mechanism is not typical for southern Italy, however it is kinematically consistent with the Apennines extension. These authors conclude that the 2002 earthquakes may help to explain several large yet poorly understood historical earthquakes located between the crest of the Apennines and the Adriatic coastline.
Galli and Molin (2004)
The Molise earthquake had an epicentral intensity of I = 7-8 MCS and a maximum intensity of I = 8-9 in San Giuliano di Puglia. The historical portion of this village, built on a marly limestone hill, had intensities of 6-7 MCS, whereas the most recently developed area, on a crest of marly clays, had intensities of I = 9-10 MCS. Considering the moderate size of the mainshock and its considerable depth, the 2002 quake datapoint intensities distribution is quite extended, showing a prominent E-W elongation.
Di Luccio et al. (2005)
They estimate the source characteristics for the major shocks of the 2002 Molise earthquakes sequence, in terms of epicentral location, focal depth, fault geometry, and seismic moment. The focal mechanisms of 15 events show pure strike-slip geometry, mainly with focal planes oriented to NS (sinistral) and EW (dextral). They suggest that the mainshock ruptured along an EW plane from the relocated aftershock distribution. These authors estimate the stress field using stress tensor inversion. The stress field shows a maximum principal stressaxis with an east-west trend, whereas the minimum stress direction is almost N-S. They suggest that several pre-existing minor faults were activated rather than a single planar fault associated with the mainshock. They suggest that the seismic strain release along the E-W fault system occurs within a zone of deformation of 10 to 30 km width. They then compute the slip distribution of the mainshock by finite fault analysis.
VallÃ©e and Di Luccio (2005)
These authors show that the two mainshocks of the Molise sequence are similar, in terms of hypocentral depth, focal mechanism, and source kinematics. The identified up-dip rupture propagation has amplified the radiation usually created by such Mw = 5.8 earthquakes at 15-20 km depth. In particular the rupture reaches about 6 km deep for the 10/31/2002 earthquake (hypocentral depth=16 km), and 9 km for the 01/11/2002 earthquake (hypocentral depth=18 km). They model a maximum acceleration zone in agreement with location of damaged villages.
Cara et al. (2005)
They use the aftershock recordings in San Giuliano di Puglia to investigate the local amplification effect due to the lateral variations of near-surface geology.
The waveform analysis shows that in the high-damage zone, where clay deposits outcrop, direct S waves are characterized by a large initial pulse that is a factor of 6 larger than S waves recorded on a nearby rock outcrop, a few hundred meters away. They show that the strong S pulse is followed by a 10-sec long amplification of ground motion between 4 and 7 Hz. This frequency band corresponds to the resonance frequencies of the most common type of construction in San Giuliano di Puglia. They conclude that the highly damaging effect in the clayey zone could have been due to the combination of the large initial pulse with time-persistent amplification at the resonant frequencies of buildings.
